stem: In the composed session, the prompt states the arithmetic in one line, gives the inputs in full, shows an example row for format, and adds one sentence of context. On OpenAI's prompt-engineering page and the CPA.com toolkit as this lesson reports them, what do those parts of the prompt do?

choices.text: They make the request clear, specific, and in context, with an example — so the response is an answer to the question actually meant — and they say nothing about whether the answer will be correct.
They guarantee correct figures, because a prompt that states the formula causes the model to calculate rather than generate.
They are optional; the page says a one-line request produces the same output as a detailed one.
They satisfy a documentation requirement the toolkit places on prompts before they are sent.

feedback: OpenAI's page says to ensure prompts are clear, specific, and provide enough context for the model to understand what you are asking; the toolkit says generative AI is only as good as the prompt that drives it, and that providing the model with examples helps get a better output. That is what the four parts do: narrow what is being asked for. Choice (b) claims something neither source says — the page says nothing about whether a better prompt yields a truer answer, and OpenAI ties accurate calculation to a tool, not to the wording of the prompt. Choice (c) contradicts both sources' advice. Choice (d) confuses the prompt with the review: the toolkit's documentation line concerns the review process for AI output, discussed with counsel, not the prompt. Re-watch S-03 and S-04, blocks 3 and 4.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md 13#3 (clear, specific, enough context), 4#8 (only as good as the prompt), 4#9 (examples help); file 13 "Does not cover" (accuracy — the page does not say a better prompt yields a truer answer) and 9#12 (accurate calculation tied to the tool) for choice (b); 4#6 (documentation of the review process, with counsel) for choice (d). Flag inherited: the session is `illustration`; the question rests on the sources' advice, not on what the composed model did.

stem: The hand recomputation for Equipment B produced one Year 3 figure and the response's table showed another. On its sources, what does this lesson say about why an ordinary response can contain a wrong figure?

choices.text: A response is based on patterns in the model's training data and can be incorrect or misleading; the toolkit's quoted executive puts it as generated output, not computed answers. The sources say nothing about how often, or why a particular figure is wrong.
The model calculated correctly and then rounded, so the difference is presentation and the table can be used as delivered.
The prompt was ambiguous about salvage value; a clearer prompt would have produced a computed figure.
The model's figure is the right one and the hand recomputation is wrong, because the model has seen more depreciation schedules than any one person.

feedback: OpenAI's page says ChatGPT provides responses based on patterns in the data it was trained on and can produce incorrect or misleading outputs; the CPA.com toolkit quotes an executive saying today's large language models produce generated output, not computed answers. That is the whole explanation the lesson offers, and no source gives an error rate or a reason for any one wrong figure. Choice (b) invents a mechanism no source describes, and a figure in a response is checked by recomputing it, not by explaining it away. Choice (c) puts the cause in the prompt, which stated the arithmetic in one line; the page says nothing about accuracy following from prompt wording, and OpenAI ties accurate calculation to a tool. Choice (d) treats the response's authority as evidence: the page says confidence is not reliability and tells users to verify important information. Re-watch S-07 and S-08, blocks 7 and 8.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md 9#1 (patterns; incorrect or misleading), 4#3 (generated output, not computed answers — attributed to Jeff Seibert, CEO of Digits); file 9 "Does not cover" (any error rate) for the last sentence of (a); 9#9 (always verify data) for choice (b); file 13 "Does not cover" and 9#12 for choice (c); 9#6 and 9#7 for choice (d). Flag inherited: the wrong figure is `illustration` (composed); the question is answerable from the sources' account of the ordinary response.

stem: The second pass, asked to run the arithmetic in the data analysis tool, returned the same Year 3 figure the participant had computed by hand. On this lesson's account, what made that figure one the participant could rely on?

choices.text: That the figure was computed by the tool and recomputed outside the conversation, and the two agree — either the tool computing a figure or an outside recomputation is what settles it, and here both happened.
The second table on its own: a response produced with the tool needs no further check.
That the model corrected itself when told it was wrong, which shows the first figure was a one-off.
Nothing further was needed once the tool was named in the prompt, since naming the tool guarantees it ran.

feedback: OpenAI's page ties accurate calculation to the code tool and, separately, says always to verify data; lesson 1's rule puts the two together: if a number matters, either the tool computed it or it is recomputed somewhere else before it is relied on. In the session both happened and they agreed, and the lesson says that agreement, not the second table alone, is what settles the figure. Choice (b) drops the first-draft rule, which the page states for every response. Choice (c) reads a conclusion no source supports: nothing in the sources says how often a figure is wrong or why, so one corrected pass shows nothing about the first. Choice (d) assumes a fact the lesson says its sources do not give — how a plan exposes the tool, or how to tell from the screen that it ran. Re-watch S-09 and S-10, blocks 9 and 10.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md 9#12 (accurate calculations tied to the tool), 9#9 (always verify data), 9#8 (first draft, not a final source) for choice (b); file 9 "Does not cover" (error rate) for choice (c); file 9 "Does not cover" and guide/03/05-calculation.md's closing paragraph (how to prompt for the tool and how to tell it ran are not stated) for choice (d). Flag inherited: the depiction of the tool running is `illustration`.

stem: A participant asks ChatGPT, in an ordinary conversation, for a straight-line depreciation schedule, with the arithmetic spelled out in the prompt, and receives a tidy table in the format requested. Before any figure from that table goes into a working paper, what does this lesson require?

choices.text: Treat the table as a first draft: recompute the figures from the inputs, or have the arithmetic run in the code tool, and rely on a figure only when it was computed or recomputed, and the two agree.
Confirm that the table matches the format the prompt asked for; a response that followed the format has followed the arithmetic.
Ask the model to confirm that its figures are correct; a confident confirmation is sufficient verification.
Use the table as delivered, because the prompt stated the formula and the model applies a stated formula exactly.

feedback: OpenAI's page says to use ChatGPT as a first draft, not a final source, and always to verify data; it ties accurate calculation to the code tool, not to the ordinary response. The lesson's rule follows: a figure is relied on when it was computed or recomputed, not when it looks right. Choice (b) confuses format with figures: the composed session's first table was in exactly the requested format and one figure in it was wrong. Choice (c) asks the response to vouch for itself; the page says the model may sound confident even when it is wrong and that confidence is not reliability. Choice (d) is the claim the toolkit's quoted executive denies — generated output, not computed answers — and the page's own description of the ordinary response as based on patterns that can be incorrect. Re-watch S-06, S-07 and S-10, blocks 6, 7 and 10.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md 9#8 (first draft), 9#9 (always verify data), 9#12 (calculation tied to the tool); 9#2 and 9#6 for choice (c); 4#3 (attributed) and 9#1 for choice (d); the composed session's S-05 for choice (b). Flag inherited: none — the question rests on the sources' rule, and the session is used only as the example of format without correctness.

stem: In the composed session this lesson walks through, where did the model's output require correction, and how was that point found?

choices.text: One cell of the first table — the Year 3 figure for Equipment B — found by recomputing that asset's annual charge by hand from the prompt's inputs and comparing the result with the table.
The example row in the prompt, found when the model reproduced it in the table as a fourth asset.
The whole first table, found because the response cited no source for its figures.
Nothing required correction; the second pass was run only to confirm that the first table was right.

feedback: The correction was to one figure, and it was found the way the page says data is verified: by recomputing it. The participant took one asset, did the arithmetic the prompt had stated, and compared the result with the table; eight cells matched and one did not. Choice (b) describes something that did not happen and mistakes the example row, which the prompt marked as format only, for an input. Choice (c) looks for the wrong kind of evidence: a schedule computed from the prompt's own inputs has no external record to cite, so the check for it is arithmetic, not a citation, and most of the table was right. Choice (d) contradicts what was on screen: the first table's Year 3 figure for Equipment B was labelled wrong, and the second pass was asked for because of it. Re-watch S-07 and S-08, blocks 7 and 8.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md 9#9 (always verify data; the check by recomputing is guide/06/02-what-is-always-verified.md's account of it), 4#9 (the example row, for choice (b)), 13#4 (review the response, refine the prompt — why the second pass was asked for, for choice (d)). Flag inherited: the session is `illustration`; the question asks about the session as shown, which is what lo-1's "identify where the model's output required correction" measures.
